item_title: Preprint: the problem with average soil temperature
item_introduction: Priya Nair's new model suggests a warmer average matters less than how often the soil crosses freezing.

add_image.image_alt: Hands holding a sample of dark surface soil
add_image.image_caption: Surface soil from the northern warming plots, sampled after the 2026 thaw.

add_paragraph: Most soil-carbon models summarise a year with one number: the mean temperature. Priya Nair's preprint, posted this week on **EGUsphere**, argues that the mean hides the part a root actually experiences — how often the soil crosses 0 °C, and how fast it swings between freeze and thaw.

The model was tuned on four years of labelling data from the **Storglommen** plots and a new hourly temperature record from three depths. It reproduces the measured carbon loss only when the freeze–thaw cycle is included: plots with the same annual mean but more crossings lost up to **37% more fresh root carbon** over a season.

“We are not saying mean warming is irrelevant,” Nair said. “We are saying it is an incomplete summary.” The preprint is open for discussion until January, and the labelled-core data behind it is already on the open-data portal.
